questions.prompt: A safelisted cross-origin POST reached the API and the browser blocked response access. What can have happened?

options.label: The server may already have changed state; inspect server evidence.
CORS automatically rolled the operation back.
A blocked response proves no request was sent.

questions.explanation: For this request shape, sending precedes the response-sharing check. CORS does not roll back server effects and an unreadable response cannot prove absence of mutation.

questions.prompt: A custom-header operation requires preflight and that preflight fails. What follows for the browser?

options.label: It does not send that guarded operation after this failed preflight.
It sends the operation anyway but hides only the response.
This proves all other request shapes are blocked.

questions.explanation: The failed required preflight prevents this operation. That differs from response blocking after a safelisted request, and does not establish behavior for other request shapes.

questions.prompt: An allowed-origin request has a valid session and CSRF proof but targets another user’s object. What must the server still do?

options.label: Check authorization for that actor, object and operation.
Trust the origin as proof that the actor owns the object.
Treat the CSRF token as permission to every object.

questions.explanation: Neither allowed response-sharing origin nor valid anti-forgery proof grants object access. Authentication identifies an actor; authorization checks the requested operation.

questions.prompt: When reviewing a cross-site session attack, what assumption must be checked?

options.label: Whether the browser’s actual cookie and request policies permit the credentials to be sent.
Cookies are always sent on every cross-site request.
Cookies can never be sent on cross-site requests.

questions.explanation: Cookie attributes, browser policies and request context affect credential sending. Both absolute claims erase assumptions required by a concrete trace.
